Seminar Title:

The Censor Within: Literary Censorship and Dissent in Postcolonial India, 1975–Present

Seminar Type:

Synopsis Seminar

Department:

Humanities and Social Sciences

Speaker Name:

Fujeena Abdul Kader ( Rollno : 518hs1013)

Speaker Type:

Student

Venue:

HS Seminar Room (MN436)

Date and Time:

12 May 2026 10.00AM

Contact:

Upender Gundala

Abstract:

This thesis examines the evolution of literary censorship in India from the Emergency of 1975&ndash77 to the present, arguing that censorship in postcolonial India must be understood not merely as a mechanism of suppression but as a productive force that has reshaped authorship, literary form, and the conditions under which dissent is expressed. The study traces this evolution across three distinct historical phases: the Emergency period, in which pre-publication clearance, surveillance, and institutional compliance turned silence into a survival strategy for writers the decade of liberalisation and intensified identity politics (1991&ndash2000), in which censorship shifted from the state to non-state actors operating through public outrage, moral policing, communal mobilisation, and market withdrawal and the contemporary phase (2001&ndashpresent), in which censorship has become digitally amplified and participatory, driven as much by social media vilification and algorithmic circulation as by formal legal prohibition.

The study develops the original concept of censorship subjectivity as its central theoretical contribution: the condition in which writers internalise the anticipation of backlash and reorganise their creative practice in response, producing literary forms that are neither simple silence nor open resistance. Drawing on Foucault&rsquos account of the author-function (1977) and Bourdieu&rsquos sociology of the literary field (1993), and informed by media studies scholarship on echo chambers, algorithmic amplification, and decontextualised circulation, the concept names the internal mechanism through which the chilling effect documented in existing scholarship is produced and reproduced.

Through close reading of selected literary texts, authorial accounts, court judgements, and paratextual materials, the thesis examines case studies including Khushwant Singh, O.V. Vijayan, and Nayantara Sahgal in the Emergency period Salman Rushdie, Taslima Nasrin, Bama, and Arundhati Roy in the liberalisation decade and Perumal Murugan, Hansda Sowvendra Shekhar, and S. Hareesh in the digital era. Across these cases, the study shows that censorial pressure has consistently generated new literary forms, new modes of authorship, and new vocabularies of resistance.

Keywords: literary censorship postcolonial India censorship subjectivity productive censorship participatory digital censorship literary dissent
